subtype: Approach: choosing a few high-impact goals [Thinking]
passage: Mentoring note, Ira. Sonali came to our monthly one-to-one with a single page: two projects, the churn dashboard and the onboarding revamp, both tied to the team's target for the year. When I asked why not the three others on her plate, she explained aloud that these two were what the promotion criteria measure: results the team can point to. Halfway through, a colleague messaged her for help with a slide deck. Sonali replied politely, "Not this month, but here's a template that might help." She glanced at me and shrugged. What I did next: I moved one small recurring task of hers to another team and asked her to bring me anything unclear about priorities. Three months later both projects had numbers beside them.

qa.q: Which two projects did Sonali choose?
qa.a: Sonali chose the churn dashboard and the onboarding revamp.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she declined the colleague's request?
qa.a: Sonali was probably a little uneasy about saying no but stayed firm and polite, glancing at Ira and shrugging.

qa.q: What else could Sonali do to keep her focus, and why?
qa.a: Sonali could keep a short list of what she has declined and why, because it helps her explain her priorities to her manager.

qa.q: How might the colleague who asked for help have seen the polite refusal?
qa.a: The colleague may feel a bit disappointed, but the template offered in reply shows that Sonali still cares about helping.

grounding: Illustrates picking two projects tied to team targets, politely declining smaller requests and delivering clear results that match promotion criteria.

subtype: Approach: reviewing feedback and adjusting the timeline [Revision]
passage: In the district bank's small IT office, Rashmi said quietly, "Ajay, your technical work is strong, but I haven't yet seen leadership." Ajay had hoped this would be his cycle. He walked to the tea stall across the road and drank slowly, watching the bus stand. "If leadership is what they want to see, one cycle isn't enough to show it," he told himself. Back at his desk he wrote a new plan: mentor the new intern, Prabha, from the first of next month, and lead the demo for the regional heads in March. He would aim for the next cycle instead. He showed the plan to Rashmi, who asked him to review it with her every month.

qa.q: Who did Ajay plan to mentor?
qa.a: Ajay planned to mentor the new intern, Prabha.

qa.q: How did Ajay feel when Rashmi said leadership had not yet been seen?
qa.a: Ajay felt disappointed, having hoped it would be his cycle, and needed time alone at the tea stall to take it in.

qa.q: What else could Ajay do to show leadership, and why?
qa.a: Ajay could take on organising the team's weekly planning, because guiding others in a small everyday task also counts as leadership.

qa.q: How might the intern Prabha benefit from Ajay's plan?
qa.a: Prabha would probably feel supported and learn faster, with a mentor who has time set aside for the role.

grounding: Illustrates hearing that leadership is not yet shown, letting go of the current cycle and planning to mentor an intern and lead a demo for the next one.

subtype: Approach: comparing with a peer's path without context [Pitfall]
passage:
Indu: You copied a colleague's promotion path?

Gurleen: Every step. Yogesh got promoted in two years: a training course, one big presentation, then a move to the platform team. So I took the same course, gave the same kind of presentation, and asked for the same move. Two years went by. Nothing. I was angry, then confused, and only then did I look at what was different. His team had doubled in size and three senior posts had opened. Mine hasn't grown in years, so there was no senior post to move into. He followed a path that fitted his team. I followed his path in a team where it led nowhere.

qa.q: How long did it take Yogesh to be promoted?
qa.a: Yogesh got promoted in two years.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when nothing happened after two years?
qa.a: Gurleen was angry and then confused, until seeing what was different.

qa.q: What else could Gurleen do to plan a promotion, and why?
qa.a: Gurleen could ask the manager what senior posts might open in this team and build a plan from that, because the path has to fit where the team is heading.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have seen his own promotion?
qa.a: Yogesh probably saw it as the result of his own effort and did not think about how much the growing team helped.

grounding: Illustrates copying a colleague's promotion steps without noticing that the colleague's team was growing and the narrator's was not, so the same path gives no equal opportunity.

subtype: Approach: mock interview with a mentor before the panel [Action]
passage:
Day 1, nine days before the panel. Aadhya's draft was neat: attended the weekly sync, wrote monthly reports, handled client tickets, supported two projects.

Day 3. She read it to her mentor Vikas over coffee. Vikas listened, then said, "You've told me what you did. I still don't know what changed because of it." Aadhya's cheeks went warm.

Day 6. She rewrote the whole page around results: cut monthly reporting from three days to one, which freed the analysts for project work, and brought in two client accounts.

Day 9. The panel asked follow-up questions about the results, not about her schedule.

qa.q: How long did monthly reporting take after Aadhya's change?
qa.a: Monthly reporting went from three days to one.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when the mentor said it was unclear what had changed?
qa.a: Aadhya felt embarrassed and stung, and her cheeks went warm, but the comment showed her what the panel would want.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya do before the panel, and why?
qa.a: Aadhya could ask Vikas to run one more mock round with tough questions, because practice answering out loud makes results easier to explain.

qa.q: How might the panel see the rewritten case?
qa.a: The panel probably finds it clearer and more convincing, since results and outcomes are easier to judge than a list of tasks.

grounding: Illustrates presenting a promotion case to a mentor before the panel, hearing that it lists tasks instead of impact, and rewriting it around results.

subtype: Approach: researching market ranges and gathering evidence [Thinking]
passage: Mentor's note, Payal. Hafsa came to me on Wednesday, three days before her offer discussion. She had already done her homework: printed salary ranges for developer roles in Pune from three sources, messaged two former batchmates about what they were paid, and listed her skills with one example each. On a sticky note she wrote two numbers: a hoped-for figure, and a floor she would accept. "The floor is so I don't say yes when I'm nervous," she told me. I asked only one question: what will you do if they offer below the minimum? She said she would ask for a day to think. I told her to bring the note to the call, and I will check in with her that evening.

qa.q: Which city's salary ranges did Hafsa check?
qa.a: Hafsa printed salary ranges for developer roles in Pune.

qa.q: What was Hafsa afraid of when writing the lower number?
qa.a: Hafsa was afraid of saying yes just because she was nervous.

qa.q: What else could Hafsa do on the call, and why?
qa.a: Hafsa could ask what the range is for the role before naming a number, because it shows what the company has planned.

qa.q: How might the recruiter see a candidate who comes prepared like this?
qa.a: The recruiter may find the talk easier and more honest, since the candidate's numbers and skills are backed by evidence.

grounding: Illustrates a developer checking market salary ranges, asking peers, listing her skills and setting a target and a minimum before an offer discussion.

subtype: Approach: deciding the walk-away point beforehand [Thinking]
passage:
Kiran: You're the man who didn't cave. How?

Hemant: Before the call, I sat with a notebook and decided the lowest overall package I'd accept, plus the other things I cared about: remote days and a learning budget. I wrote it down. Because in the room, when the recruiter says "this is our best offer" and waits, the silence feels like an emergency. I had agreed with myself: no answer below the line on the spot. When the moment came, I said, "I'd like to think it over and reply by tomorrow evening." My hands were sweating, but I wasn't deciding with the sweat. I was deciding with the notebook.

qa.q: What else besides pay did Hemant write down as mattering?
qa.a: Hemant wrote down remote days and a learning budget.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when the recruiter waited in silence?
qa.a: Hemant felt pressured, as the silence felt like an emergency and the hands were sweating.

qa.q: What else could Hemant do after saying the reply would come tomorrow evening, and why?
qa.a: Hemant could compare the offer with the written line calmly at home and answer as promised, because a decision made without pressure is easier to trust.

qa.q: How might the recruiter have seen the request to reply the next evening?
qa.a: The recruiter may find it reasonable and professional, seeing a candidate who takes the decision seriously.

grounding: Illustrates deciding beforehand the lowest total package and what else matters, so that agreeing to an offer under pressure is avoided.

passage:
Saturday. Practised with Imran for an hour on the terrace. Imran played the recruiter and, when I asked for a higher base, said in a flat voice, "The budget is fixed." My mind went blank the first time. The second time I said, "I understand. Is there any room on a joining bonus, or on a review after six months?" The third time it came out smooth. Imran told me my voice went up at the end of every sentence, so I recorded myself and listened. It's odd hearing yourself ask for money. Tomorrow one more round, and then I stop. It feels ridiculous, and it also feels like the only way to walk in steady.

Nazia

qa.q: How long did Nazia practise with Imran?
qa.a: Nazia practised for an hour on the terrace.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel the first time Imran said the budget was fixed?
qa.a: Nazia felt flustered, with a mind that went blank, before managing a calmer reply the second time.

qa.q: What else could Nazia do to prepare, and why?
qa.a: Nazia could write down the preferred reply and keep it beside the phone, because a written line is easy to find if the mind goes blank again.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt playing the recruiter?
qa.a: Imran may have felt a little awkward being so flat and firm, but likely wanted to be helpful.

grounding: Illustrates rehearsing a salary conversation aloud with a friend, including the moment when the budget is said to be fixed, and preparing a calm reply.

passage: In a glass meeting room in Lisbon, Olga from HR slid the offer across the table. The base salary was firm. Paulo had expected that. "I understand the base is set," he said. "Could we talk about the rest? A joining bonus, a review after six months, and two days a week working from home." Olga tapped her pen, then stepped into the corridor to make a call. Ten minutes later she was back. The bonus was possible, and so was the review in six months, but the home days would have to wait. "Two out of three," she said. Paulo smiled and asked for it in writing. They shook hands, and Olga looked as relieved as he felt.

qa.q: Which two requests did the company agree to?
qa.a: The company agreed to the joining bonus and the review in six months.

qa.q: How did Paulo feel at the end of the meeting?
qa.a: Paulo felt relieved and pleased, since two of his three requests were agreed.

qa.q: What else could Paulo do before starting the job, and why?
qa.a: Paulo could check the written terms carefully and ask again about home days after the review, because writing avoids later misunderstanding and the issue may be easier once he has shown his value.

qa.q: How might Olga have seen Paulo's approach?
qa.a: Olga may have appreciated a calm, specific request that respected the firm base, which made it easier to say yes to part of it.

grounding: Illustrates accepting a firm base and negotiating the whole package: a joining bonus, a six-month review and home days, of which two are agreed.

subtype: Approach: accepting the first offer from fear of losing it [Pitfall]
passage:
Yash: You started in March too, right? Same level as me?
Hansa: Yes. Level two.
Yash: What did they offer you? I only ask because I found out they told me a lot more than I expected.
Hansa: I didn't ask. They phoned on Friday and I said yes before they'd finished the sentence. I thought if I hesitated it would disappear.
Yash: Nothing at all? Not one question?
Hansa: Not one. I could have asked about a joining bonus, or a review. I keep thinking about that.
Yash: Mine is quite a bit more than you told me yours is.
Hansa: I know. I saw the pay slip mix-up. It stung.
Yash: It's done. But next time, ask one thing. Only one.
Hansa: One. Okay.

qa.q: When did the company phone Hansa with the offer?
qa.a: The company phoned Hansa on Friday.

qa.q: What is Hansa feeling now about accepting so fast?
qa.a: Hansa feels regret and a sting, thinking that even one question should have been asked.

qa.q: What could Hansa do next time, and why?
qa.a: Hansa could ask one clear question, such as about a joining bonus or a review, because asking rarely makes an offer vanish and can improve it.

qa.q: How might Yash feel about telling Hansa?
qa.a: Yash probably feels awkward and sympathetic, wanting to help Hansa learn from it rather than feel worse.

grounding: Illustrates accepting the first offer at once for fear of losing it, then learning colleagues at the same level were paid more and regretting not asking.

subtype: Approach: anchoring on a personal need instead of value [Pitfall]
passage: The offer expired at six, and the café Bhupen had picked for the call was so noisy he had to press the phone to his ear. Keerthana, from HR, said the figure. Bhupen took a breath. "That's lower than I need," he said. "My rent went up, and I have a loan with a fixed monthly payment. With those, I need more." There was a pause. "I understand," Keerthana said, "but pay is set by the role, not by personal costs. Can you tell me what you would bring to the role beyond what is in the offer?" Bhupen fumbled. He had prepared the rent and the loan, not the value. The call ended on the same figure, and a sentence he replayed all the way home on the bus.

qa.q: What reasons did Bhupen give for wanting a higher figure?
qa.a: Bhupen gave his rent going up and a loan with a fixed monthly payment.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when asked what he would bring to the role?
qa.a: Bhupen was flustered and unprepared, since he had prepared his costs but not his value.

qa.q: What could Bhupen have prepared instead, and why?
qa.a: Bhupen could have prepared examples of results he would bring and market ranges for the role, because employers weigh contribution rather than personal costs.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have heard Bhupen's argument?
qa.a: Keerthana heard need rather than contribution, so the reply stayed polite but could not move the figure.

grounding: Illustrates arguing for a higher salary figure because of rent and a loan rather than the value brought, so the employer hears need and not contribution.
